name: Lenca de Honduras / Honduran Lenca
confidence_why: Herranz 1987, recording the last semi-speaker of Guajiquiro, and King 2016 and 2017, working from the nineteenth- and twentieth-century wordlists, independently conclude that Honduran Lenca had no fixed or contrastive word stress, the accent shifting between repetitions with a tendency to fall on the last syllable of the utterance, and nothing read contradicts this, though the language is extinct and both authors call their evidence thin.
catalog_citation: King, Alan R. 2017. Lenca for Linguists (Sketch of an indigenous language of Honduras). Tushik, 44 pp. DOI 10.13140/RG.2.2.14756.17285, pp. 16 and 20.
catalog_quote: p. 16: "Stress in Honduran Lenca is poorly documented and open to conjecture. It is thought that perhaps word-stress was weak or absent and phonological phrases tended to be stressed on the final syllable.17" [n. 17: "In Chilanga Lenca, on the contrary, phrasal stress regularly falls on the penultimate syllable with few exceptions."] || p. 20: "The source data contain scanty and sometimes contradictory evidence making it hard to draw firm conclusions about the nature and placement of stress. Probably most verb forms were stressed on the last syllable; it is to be borne in mind that given Lenca's SOV syntax, the verb typically stands last in its clause, so this would actually be the last syllable of the clause. It is plausible that stress was assigned to syntactic groups rather than to individual words. It is assumed that fluid vowels were unstressed, e.g. nap ['naba], umal [u'mali]."
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: Herranz: "Lenca stress is not phonemic and, in general, it seems that in Honduran Lenca it does not have as fixed a position as Campbell reports for Salvadoran Lenca (on the penultimate syllable). Our informant, when repeating a word, frequently changes the position of the stress: poriná/porínia, ..., etc. Oxytone endings in -úh, -éh, -án, -én and -ín abound, as do nominal and verbal endings in stressed -í."

new_statements.rule_in_words: No fixed or contrastive word stress can be established. The one first-hand observer (Herranz, recording a 75-year-old semi-speaker from Guajiquiro in 1983) says stress is not phonemic, varies between repetitions of the same word, and that final-stressed word shapes are frequent. King's philological reconstruction from the 19th-20th-century wordlists (2016, 2017) finds no explicit statement in any primary source, notes that written accents fall almost always on the last syllable and are inconsistent for the same word, and proposes as a hypothesis that word stress was weak or absent and that the phonological phrase (typically ending in the SOV clause-final verb) was stressed on its final syllable; penultimate stress in some words is not excluded, antepenultimate is rare. Provisional catalog label: stress non-contrastive/variable with a final-syllable (phrase-final) tendency.
new_statements.exceptions: Herranz: informant shifts stress between repetitions (poriná/porínia). King 2016: laina 'está' written both laina and lainá; imperative -ta written -tá and -ta; 'fluid' final vowels (nap ~ napa, umal ~ umali) are unstressed; esdrújula (antepenult) stress rare but not absent in the corpus.
new_statements.domain_note: Herranz's observation is on isolated words elicited from a wordlist (Swadesh 400) in citation form, from one informant; King's is on the whole written corpus (wordlists plus short dialogues) and explicitly frames stress as phrase-level (clause-final predicate) rather than word-level. Contrast with Salvadoran/Chilanga Lenca (lenc1243), which has regular penultimate phrasal stress (Campbell 1976; King 2017 n. 17).
new_statements.identity_note: Honduran Lenca (lenc1242) is extinct; Herranz's 1983 recordings are of one semi-speaker (Guadalupe Corea, 75) from the municipio of Guajiquiro, La Paz (King's 'eastern' dialect), so the first-hand statement is Guajiquiro-based. King 2016/2017 describe a unified 'Lenca Unificado Moderno' built from all Honduran wordlists (Guajiquiro, Opatoro, Intibucá, Similatón, Santa Elena/Chinacla). Penultimate-stress statements in Campbell 1976, Arguedas 1988 pp. 102-103 and Lehmann 1920 p. 693 concern Salvadoran/Chilanga Lenca (lenc1243), not this language.

new_statements.quote: In the few cases where an accent is marked, it is usually on the final syllable. [...] I hypothesize that word stress was not distinctive, probably not highly salient acoustically, but with a tendency to emphasise the last syllable of an utterance, and therefore, when glossing a word, the last syllable of the gloss will usually receive emphasis given that in the context of elicitation the gloss constitutes an utterance. The fact that a stress mark is written in words ending in n merely reflects the Spanish spelling convention according to which a word ending in a stressed syllable with a final n takes an orthographic accent.

Section 'Written accents' under 'Spelling and phonology' on p. 15 contains, word for word, 'In the few cases where an accent is marked, it is usually on the final syllable.' and the full passage 'I hypothesize that word stress was not distinctive, probably not highly salient acoustically, but with a tendency to emphasise the last syllable of an utterance, and therefore, when glossing a word, the last syllable of the gloss will usually receive emphasis given that in the context of elicitation the gloss constitute…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing statements (Herranz 1987: 446, accent not phonemic and not fixed in position; King 2017: 16, 20, word stress weak or absent with phrase-final stress). Adds Similaton-dialect-specific evidence, the explicit hypothesis that stress was non-distinctive with utterance-final emphasis, the orthographic-convention explanation for final-syllable accents on -n words, and the list of non-final accented forms. The catalog record itself has an empty rule; this source supports leaving no fixed word-stress position.
new_statements.rule_in_words: King's hypothesis for Similaton Lenca (from the sporadic written accents in Membreño's 1897 wordlist): word stress was not distinctive and probably not acoustically salient; the only prominence tendency is emphasis on the last syllable of an utterance, which in elicitation makes the last syllable of a cited word sound stressed. Final-syllable accent marks on words in -n are explained away as a Spanish orthographic convention, not evidence of Lenca stress.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 15-16: an accent is occasionally written on a penultimate or antepenultimate syllable (güémap, terìgui, shúndisca, náplin); of these, three are morphologically complex and terigui is a hapax of unknown structure. moló has a written accent on a final open syllable (King suspects a dropped final n). Membreño uses acute and grave accents interchangeably, even in Spanish glosses.
new_statements.identity_note: The work opened is the Similaton (Southern Honduran Lenca) dialect profile, built from Membreño 1897 and Squier 1858 wordlists; its stress hypothesis is framed for Similaton but King applies the same reasoning to Honduran Lenca generally in his 2016 Preliminary Proposal and 2017 sketch. The Opatoro and Santa Elena profiles named in the same citation were not obtainable. Chilanga / El Salvador Lenca (penultimate stress per Campbell) is a different language and is mentioned only for contrast.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement. King 2016 (Similaton profile) and King 2017 (Lenca for Linguists) say the same thing in different words: no distinctive word stress, emphasis on the last syllable of the utterance / clause-final predicate. Herranz 1987: 446, working from a recording of one semi-speaker, says the accent is not phonemic and does not have a fixed position (the informant moves it when repeating a word, e.g. poriná/porínia), which is compatible with King. The only tension is interpretive: Herranz notes that oxytone endings in -úh, -éh, -án, -én, -ín abound, whereas King treats the final accent marks on -n words in the old wordlists as a Spanish spelling convention rather than evidence of stress. Herranz also lists (p. 437) the Mesoamerican areal 'acento tónico (énfasis)' rule V -> V́ / __C(V)# as one of the few areal traits Lenca shares, which sits oddly with his own p. 446 statement that Honduran Lenca stress is not fixed like the penultimate stress Campbell reports for Salvadoran (Chilanga) Lenca; that internal inconsistency is in a source already on record, not in the work opened here.

sources.note: p. 446: stress is not phonemic and has no fixed position in Honduran Lenca (unlike Salvadoran Lenca penult per Campbell); the informant (Guadalupe Corea, 75, Guajiquiro, recorded Feb/Aug 1983) shifts the accent when repeating a word (porina/porinia); oxytone endings -úh, -éh, -án, -én, -ín and stressed -í abound; too few phrases to say anything about intonation (p. 445). p. 436 n. 23 lists among the Mesoamerican areal traits Lenca shares the stress rule V -> V́ / __C(V)# (Campbell, Kaufman & Smith-Stark 1986 trait 22).
